claim: Ribosomes can read through stop codons in a regulated manner, elongating rather than terminating the nascent peptide.
source: Ribosomes can read through stop codons in a regulated manner, elongating rather than terminating the nascent peptide.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to prior work on viral systems and eukaryotic genes.

claim: Stop codon readthrough is essential to diverse viruses.
source: Stop codon readthrough is essential to diverse viruses
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Cimino et al., 2011; Li and Rice, 1989; Napthine et al., 2012; Skuzeski et al., 1991; Yoshinaka et al., 1985; reviewed in Beier and Grimm, 2001; Firth and Brierley, 2012)

claim: 283 readthrough events were phylogenetically predicted in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Using this approach, 283 readthrough events were predicted in Drosophila melanogaster
evidence: Cited from prior work by Lin et al., 2007 and Jungreis et al., 2011

claim: Readthrough is far more pervasive than expected, with the vast majority of readthrough events evolved within D. melanogaster and not predicted phylogenetically.
source: Readthrough is far more pervasive than expected: the vast majority of readthrough events evolved within D. melanogaster and were not predicted phylogenetically.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing 307 novel extensions not predicted phylogenetically (Figure 3A)

claim: More than 300 readthrough events not predicted by phylogenetic approaches were identified.
source: we identify more than 300 readthrough events not predicted by phylogenetic approaches
evidence: Supported by experimental ribosome profiling data showing 307 novel extensions (Figure 3A, supplementary table 2)

claim: C-terminal protein extensions resulting from readthrough show evidence of selection.
source: The resulting C-terminal protein extensions show evidence of selection
evidence: Supported by Z-curve analysis (Figure 6B) and SNP analysis (Figure 6C) showing signatures of protein-coding selection

claim: C-terminal extensions contain functional subcellular localization signals.
source: contain functional subcellular localization signals
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally by showing that extensions contain functional nuclear localization signals (Figure 7, Table 2)

claim: Readthrough is regulated between different cell types and developmental stages.
source: their readthrough is regulated, arguing for their importance
evidence: Demonstrated by differential readthrough rates between S2 cells and 0-2 hr embryos (Table 1)

claim: Readthrough occurs in yeast and humans.
source: We further demonstrate that readthrough occurs in yeast and humans.
evidence: Supported by ribosome profiling data from [psi-] yeast and human foreskin fibroblasts (Figure 5, supplementary tables 3 and 4)

claim: Drosophila ribosomes are highly sensitive to RNase I.
source: we found that Drosophila ribosomes are highly sensitive to RNase I
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally by showing ribosome degradation with RNase I digestion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)

claim: Drosophila ribosomes tolerate micrococcal nuclease (MNase) over a wide range of concentrations.
source: we found that Drosophila ribosomes tolerate micrococcal nuclease (MNase) over a wide range of concentrations
evidence: Demonstrated by stable monosome peaks across MNase concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D)

claim: Ribosome footprint density measurements are highly reproducible with an inter-replicate standard deviation of 1.07-fold.
source: we observed strong correlation between replicates (r2 = 0.998; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and an inter-replicate standard deviation of 1.07-fold
evidence: Demonstrated by replicate experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)

claim: Translation efficiency measurements between replicate embryo collections are highly reproducible (r2 = 0.946).
source: Translation efficiency measurements between replicate embryo collections are highly reproducible (r2 = 0.946; Figure 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation analysis between biological replicates shown in Figure 1C

claim: The range of translation efficiencies for different messages spans four orders of magnitude.
source: the range of translation efficiencies for different messages spans four orders of magnitude
evidence: Shown in histogram of translation efficiency (Figure 1D)

claim: Translation efficiency is uncorrelated with mRNA abundance (r2 = 8.29 × 10−5).
source: translation efficiency is uncorrelated with mRNA abundance (r2 = 8.29 × 10−5; Figure 1E)
evidence: Demonstrated by scatter plot analysis (Figure 1E)

claim: mRNA abundance predicts only one third of the variance in the rate of protein production as measured by ribosome footprint density.
source: mRNA abundance predicts only one third of the variance in the rate of protein production as measured by ribosome footprint density (Figure 1F)
evidence: Inferred from scatter plot showing relationship between ribosome density and mRNA abundance (Figure 1F)

claim: Translational regulation is a major determinant of gene expression in the early embryo.
source: Translational regulation is therefore a major determinant of gene expression in the early embryo
evidence: Inferred from the wide range of translation efficiencies and their independence from mRNA abundance (Figure 1D-F)

claim: Ribosome density on 5′ UTRs is similar to that of coding regions.
source: Ribosome density on 5′ UTRs is similar to that of coding regions
evidence: Demonstrated by histogram showing comparable ribosome footprint densities (Figure 2A)

claim: The density in 5′ UTRs is attributed to translating 80S ribosomes rather than 48S preinitiation complexes.
source: We attribute this density to translating 80S ribosomes rather than 48S preinitiation complexes
evidence: Supported by three lines of evidence: footprint length distribution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indistinguishable measurements between cushion and gradient preparations (Figure 2B), and presence of initiation peaks at uORF boundaries (Figure 2C)

claim: The length distribution of protected fragments in 5′ UTRs (25–35 nt) is indistinguishable from the length distribution in coding regions.
source: the length distribution of protected fragments in 5′ UTRs (25–35 nt) is indistinguishable from the length distribution of ribosome-protected fragments in coding regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of read length distributions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)

claim: The density of ribosomes on 3′ UTRs is several orders of magnitude lower than in coding regions and 5′ UTRs.
source: the density of ribosomes on 3′ UTRs is several orders of magnitude lower than in coding regions and 5′ UTRs
evidence: Shown in histogram of ribosome footprint density (Figure 2A)

claim: 43 of 158 expressed phylogenetically predicted extensions exhibited clear signs of readthrough in 0-2 hr embryos.
source: Of this subset, 43 exhibited clear signs of readthrough.
evidence: Reported in Venn diagram (Figure 3A) and detailed in supplementary table 2

claim: 307 examples of readthrough were identified that were not phylogenetically predicted.
source: In addition, we identified 307 examples of readthrough that were not phylogenetically predicted.
evidence: Reported in Venn diagram (Figure 3A) and detailed in supplementary table 2

claim: Footprint count measurements for each extension are highly correlated between libraries made using sucrose cushions and sucrose gradients.
source: Footprint count measurements for each extension are highly correlated between libraries made using these two sample preparation methods
evidence: Demonstrated by correlation plot (Figure 4A)

claim: Footprints in C-terminal extensions exhibit a length distribution very similar to footprints in coding regions.
source: Footprints in C-terminal extensions exhibit a length distribution very similar to footprints in coding regions
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of read length distributions (Figure 4B)

claim: C-terminal extensions exhibit peaks of ribosome density at their stop codons characteristic of translation termination.
source: C-terminal extensions exhibit peaks at their stop codons, clearly arguing that footprint density in C-terminal extensions is attributable to actively-translating ribosomes (Figure 4C)
evidence: Demonstrated by metagene analysis showing termination peaks (Figure 4C)

claim: Readthrough produces detectable protein products for at least 8 out of 15 tested extensions.
source: We detected readthrough products of the correct size for eight of the reporters
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and western blotting (Figure 4D)

claim: UGA stop codons represent only 25% of the readthrough events reported.
source: UGA stop codons represent only 25% of the readthrough events we report
evidence: Calculated from the dataset of identified readthrough events

claim: None of the UGA-containing readthrough transcripts are annotated as selenoproteins in FlyBase or SelenoDB.
source: none of these are annotated as selenoproteins in either FlyBase (Marygold et al., 2013) or SelenoDB (Castellano et al., 2008)
evidence: Determined by searching annotation databases

claim: No SECIS elements were detected in any of the UGA-containing readthrough 3′ UTRs using SeciSearch 2.19.
source: we were unable to detect SECIS elements in any of their 3′ UTRs using SeciSearch 2.19
evidence: Determined by computational analysis using SeciSearch software

claim: Only 10 nucleotide positions in stop codons showed significantly elevated mismatch rates in mRNA and footprint datasets.
source: Together, the mRNA and footprint datasets identified a total of 10 nucleotide positions whose mismatch rates significantly exceeded the average (Figure 4E,F)
evidence: Determined by statistical analysis of sequencing mismatches (Figure 4E,F)

claim: Two stop codon positions contained genomic polymorphisms that converted the stop codon to a sense codon and were excluded from further study.
source: Two (Figure 4E,F, red) contained genomic polymorphisms that converted the stop codon to a sense codon. These two transcripts were therefore excluded from further study.
evidence: Identified through mismatch analysis (Figure 4E,F)

claim: The A-site footprint dataset contains no positive evidence of RNA editing at stop codons.
source: Thus, our most stringent dataset contains no positive evidence of RNA editing.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of footprints whose A-sites have passed the stop codon (Figure 4G)

claim: All tested adenine positions in stop codons contained significantly fewer A-to-G mismatches than expected under the hypothesis of A-to-I editing.
source: all positions contained significantly fewer A-to-G mismatches than expected under the hypothesis of A-to-I editing, (Bonferonni-corrected p<<0.05 for all transcripts)
evidence: Determined by binomial test on A-site footprint data

claim: Readthrough occurs at many loci in [psi−] yeast.
source: we collected yeast datasets and examined them for empirical evidence of readthrough
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling showing extensions with triplet periodicity and examples (Figure 5A-C, supplementary table 3)

claim: 42 readthrough events were identified in human foreskin fibroblasts.
source: We identified 42 readthrough events in the human data (Figure 5D,E; full results in supplementary table 4 at Dryad: Dunn et al., 2013)
evidence: Demonstrated by ribosome profiling data from human cells (Figure 5D,E, supplementary table 4)

claim: 61.8% of novel extensions in Drosophila exceed a biologically significant readthrough rate threshold of 1.2%.
source: 61.8% of the novel extensions in Drosophila...exceeded this threshold
evidence: Calculated from readthrough rate distribution (Figure 5F)

claim: 94.7% of extensions in human foreskin fibroblasts exceed a biologically significant readthrough rate threshold of 1.2%.
source: 94.7% of the extensions in human foreskin fibroblasts...exceeded this threshold
evidence: Calculated from readthrough rate distribution (Figure 5F)

claim: 40.0% of extensions in yeast exceed a biologically significant readthrough rate threshold of 1.2%.
source: 40.0% of the extensions in yeast exceeded this threshold
evidence: Calculated from readthrough rate distribution (Figure 5F)

claim: Novel extensions show a nucleotide character intermediate between coding regions and distal 3′ UTRs.
source: novel extensions exhibit a nucleotide character intermediate between coding regions and distal 3′ UTRs (p=1.02 × 10−23, Mann-Whitney U test, distal 3′ UTR vs novel extensions)
evidence: Demonstrated by Z-curve classifier analysis (Figure 6B)

claim: Novel extensions show a modest but significant preference for synonymous SNPs above the background level of distal 3′ UTRs.
source: Novel extensions show a modest but significant preference for synonymous SNPs above the background level of distal 3′ UTRs (Figure 6C; p=1.42 × 10−5, one-sided Fisher's exact test)
evidence: Demonstrated by SNP analysis (Figure 6C)

claim: Nine of 182 testable transcripts significantly change readthrough rates between S2 cells and 0-2 hr embryos.
source: we found nine of 182 testable transcripts to significantly change between samples
evidence: Determined by Fisher's exact test with FDR control (Table 1)

claim: Four transcripts show significant increases in readthrough rate in embryos compared to S2 cells.
source: We identified four significant increases...in readthrough rate in embryos compared to S2 cells
evidence: Reported in Table 1

claim: Five transcripts show significant decreases in readthrough rate in embryos compared to S2 cells.
source: We identified...five significant decreases in readthrough rate in embryos compared to S2 cells
evidence: Reported in Table 1

claim: Readthrough is regulated on a transcript-by-transcript basis.
source: indicating that readthrough is at least in part regulated on a transcript-by-transcript basis
evidence: Inferred from the observation of both increases and decreases in readthrough rates between cell types (Table 1)

claim: 10 proteins not annotated as nuclear in FlyBase contain predicted NLSes in their extensions.
source: 10 proteins not annotated as nuclear in FlyBase contain predicted NLSes in their extensions
evidence: Identified by computational prediction using cNLS mapper (Table 2)

claim: Eight extensions contain predicted transmembrane domains.
source: Eight extensions contain predicted transmembrane domains
evidence: Identified by computational prediction using TmHmm (Table 2)

claim: One extension contains a C-terminal prenylation signal.
source: one contains a C-terminal prenylation signal
evidence: Identified by computational prediction using PrePS (Table 2)

claim: One extension contains a PTS1 peroxisomal localization signal.
source: PTS1 signals were detected in one extension
evidence: Identified by computational prediction using PTS1 Predictor (Table 2)

claim: Three tested extensions contain functional NLSes that relocalize a reporter to the nucleus.
source: Three extensions also contain functional NLSes which at least partially relocalize the reporter to the nucleus when constitutively fused to it (remaining columns)
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy showing nuclear localization of GFP reporters (Figure 7)

claim: The 350 readthrough events reported represent a small subset of a larger group that occur throughout the lifetime of an individual fly.
source: we believe the 350 readthrough events we report here to represent a small subset of a larger group that occur throughout the lifetime of an individual fly
evidence: Inferred from the observation of large magnitude regulation of readthrough between cell types

claim: Many phylogenetically predicted extensions that were not observed are likely translated at other developmental stages in Drosophila.
source: We therefore expect many of the extensions that were phylogenetically predicted but not observed in our samples are in fact translated at other developmental stages in Drosophila
evidence: Inferred from the observation of regulated readthrough between cell types

claim: The true number of transcripts whose readthrough rates are regulated in tissue- or condition-specific manners is larger than reported.
source: we surmise that our ability to detect regulation was limited by sequencing depth and that the true number of transcripts whose readthrough rates are regulated in tissue- or condition-specific manners is in fact larger than we report
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcripts with significant p values have higher read counts than those without

claim: Stop codon readthrough provides a mechanism for proteins to evolve at the C-terminus.
source: we propose, along with the Lindquist (True and Lindquist, 2000) and Kellis (Jungreis et al., 2011) groups, that stop codon readthrough can provide a mechanism for proteins to evolve at the C-terminus
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by multiple lines of evidence including selection signatures, functional signals in extensions, and regulated readthrough

claim: Non-zero readthrough rates (0.02–1.4%) have been observed for control non-readthrough reporter constructs in [psi−] yeast and mammalian cells.
source: non-zero readthrough rates (0.02–1.4%) have been observed even for control non-readthrough reporter constructs in [psi−] yeast (Fearon et al., 1994; Bonetti et al., 1995; Namy et al., 2002; Keeling et al., 2004; Torabi and Kruglyak, 2011) and mammalian cells (Firth et al., 2011; Napthine et al., 2012)
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies

claim: Roughly 30% of randomly-generated peptide sequences are functional in that they can relocalize invertase in yeast.
source: a large proportion—roughly 30%—of randomly-generated peptide sequences are functional, insofar as they can relocalize a cytosolic form of invertase to the nucleus, mitochondrion, or endoplasmic reticulum in yeast (Kaiser et al., 1987; Kaiser and Botstein, 1990)
evidence: Cited from Kaiser and Botstein studies

claim: The median readthrough rate for conserved extensions in Drosophila is 5.2%.
source: the median readthrough rate for the conserved extensions in Drosophila is 5.2%
evidence: Calculated from the dataset of readthrough rates

claim: The median readthrough rate for novel extensions in Drosophila is 1.7%.
source: the median for the novel extensions is 1.7%
evidence: Calculated from the dataset of readthrough rates

claim: Ribosome profiling maps the physical positions of ribosomes on each transcript.
source: ribosome profiling maps the physical positions of ribosomes on each transcript
evidence: This is an established property of the ribosome profiling technique

claim: MNase has a strong 3′ A/T bias that gives rise to positional uncertainty with P-site mapping.
source: MNase has a strong 3′ A/T bias. This gives rise to a small amount of positional uncertainty with P-site mapping in MNase datasets
evidence: This is stated as an observed property of MNase digestion

claim: RNase I shows little cutting bias and offers superior spatial resolution along mRNAs compared to MNase.
source: In contrast to MNase (which exhibits a 3′ A/T cutting bias, yielding positional uncertainty of the ribosomal P-site, see 'Materials and methods'), RNAse I shows little cutting bias. Therefore, libraries prepared with RNase I (e.g., yeast and mammalian libraries) offer superior spatial resolution along mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as an established property of RNase I

claim: Ribosome-protected footprint fragments in coding regions exhibit a characteristic three-nucleotide periodicity or 'phasing' in RNase I-prepared libraries.
source: the locations of ribosome-protected footprint fragments in coding regions exhibit a characteristic three-nucleotide periodicity or 'phasing'
evidence: Demonstrated in yeast and human data (Figure 5A)

claim: Putative C-terminal extensions in yeast and human datasets show triplet periodicity characteristic of translation.
source: Triplet periodicity of 28-mers from yeast data in all non-overlapping coding regions (CDS), putative C-terminal extensions, and distal 3' UTRs indicates that a signature of translation readthrough is visible in extensions on a bulk scale
evidence: Demonstrated by phasing analysis (Figure 5A)

claim: The distribution of novel extensions' PhyloCSF scores is not substantially different from the global distribution of all potential extensions.
source: The distribution of novel extensions is not substantially different from the global distribution, suggesting that many of these extensions are not phylogenetically conserved beyond melanogaster
evidence: Shown in histogram of PhyloCSF scores (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)

claim: Predicted extensions show a nucleotide character indistinguishable from annotated coding regions according to Z-curve analysis.
source: Consistent with a long history of protein-coding selection, extensions predicted by phylogenetic conservation showed a nucleotide character indistinguishable from annotated coding regions (Figure 6B)
evidence: Demonstrated by Z-curve classifier (Figure 6B)

claim: The shift in Z-curve scores for novel extensions is not due to polyadenylation signals.
source: This effect is not due to specific nucleotide signals found in distal 3′ UTRs (p=3.81 × 10−22, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Demonstrated by training classifier excluding last 50 bases of UTR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)

claim: Novel extensions show a lower preference for synonymous SNPs than predicted extensions.
source: Novel extensions show...a modest but significant preference for synonymous SNPs...below that of the predicted extensions (p=8.42 × 10−9, one-sided Fisher's exact test)
evidence: Demonstrated by SNP analysis (Figure 6C)

claim: At least a fraction of the novel extensions are of recent evolutionary origin and have come under selection within the melanogaster lineage.
source: Together, these results favor the hypothesis that at least a fraction of the novel extensions are of recent evolutionary origin and have come under selection within the melanogaster lineage
evidence: Inferred from Z-curve and SNP analyses showing intermediate coding character and synonymous SNP preference

claim: The distribution of fold-changes in readthrough rate between cell types spans several orders of magnitude.
source: The distribution of fold-changes in readthrough rate spans several orders of magnitude
evidence: Observed in Table 1 showing log10 fold changes ranging from -2.46 to 0.82

claim: Transcripts with significant p values for differential readthrough are statistically more highly counted in their extensions than those without significant p values.
source: transcripts with significant p values are statistically more highly counted in their extensions than those without significant p values (p=2.4 × 10−3, Mann-Whitney U test)
evidence: Determined by statistical comparison

claim: Readthrough provides general mechanisms both to regulate gene expression and function, and to add plasticity to the proteome during evolution.
source: Readthrough thus provides general mechanisms both to regulate gene expression and function, and to add plasticity to the proteome during evolution
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including regulated readthrough, functional signals, and evolutionary signatures

claim: In early (0–2 hr) Drosophila embryos, the vast majority of transcripts are maternally supplied.
source: In early (0–2 hr) Drosophila embryos, the vast majority of transcripts are maternally supplied
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development

claim: The early Drosophila embryo has been an important system for the study of post-transcriptional and translational regulation.
source: The early Drosophila embryo has thus been an important system for the study of post-transcriptional and specifically translational regulation (reviewed in Lasko, 2011)
evidence: Cited from review by Lasko, 2011

claim: A subset of ribosomes partition into heavy polysomes in 0-2 hr embryos.
source: Figure 1A shows polysome peaks in undigested embryo lysate that collapse to monosome peak after MNase digestion
evidence: Shown in sucrose gradient profile (Figure 1A)

claim: Digestion of exposed mRNA between ribosomes collapses polysome peaks into the monosomal (80S) peak.
source: Digestion of exposed mRNA between ribosomes collapses the polysome peaks into the monosomal (80S) peak
evidence: Demonstrated in sucrose gradient (Figure 1A)

claim: The area under the monosome peak in digested samples is 1.04-fold the combined area under monosome and polysome peaks in undigested samples, indicating quantitative recovery.
source: The area under the monosome peak in the digested sample is 1.04-fold the combined area under the monosome and polysome peaks in the undigested sample, indicating quantitative recovery
evidence: Calculated from sucrose gradient profiles (Figure 1A)

claim: The standard deviation of fold-changes in translation efficiency between biological replicates is 1.19-fold.
source: The standard deviation of fold-changes between biological replicates is 1.19-fold (Figure 1C, inset)
evidence: Calculated from replicate data (Figure 1C inset)

claim: The ribosome profiling assay allows detection of even modest changes in translation efficiency.
source: allowing detection of even modest changes in translation efficiency
evidence: Inferred from the low standard deviation (1.19-fold) between replicates

claim: Initiation peaks are visible at the starts of uORFs starting with ATG and near-cognate TTG codons in Ino80.
source: Initiation peaks are visible at the starts of uORFs starting with an ATG codon (green box) and a near-cognate TTG codon (yellow box) as well as at the annotated start codon
evidence: Shown in genome browser track for Ino80 (Figure 2C)

claim: Initiation and termination of translation are slow compared to elongation.
source: Because initiation and termination of translation are slow compared to elongation, initiation and termination events produce peaks of ribosome density
evidence: This is established knowledge about translation kinetics, supported by citation to Ingolia et al., 2011

claim: 256 of 283 phylogenetically predicted extensions were consistent with FlyBase genome annotation revision 5.43.
source: Of 283 predicted extensions, 256 were consistent with FlyBase genome annotation revision 5.43
evidence: Reported in Venn diagram (Figure 3A)

claim: 158 of the 256 annotation-consistent predicted extensions had their corresponding coding regions expressed in 0–2 hr embryos.
source: For 158 of these, the corresponding coding regions were expressed in 0–2 hr embryos
evidence: Reported in Venn diagram (Figure 3A)

claim: Several transcripts contain 3′ UTR footprint density more consistent with ribosomal frameshift than readthrough.
source: we identified several transcripts that contained 3′ UTR footprint density more consistent with ribosomal frameshift (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: Examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Some transcripts show 3′ UTR footprint density consistent with the presence of additional downstream cistrons, RNA structure, or protein binding rather than readthrough.
source: we identified several transcripts that contained 3′ UTR footprint density more consistent with...the presence of additional downstream cistrons, RNA structure, or protein binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: Examples shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Stop codon peaks are missing from S2 cell samples because terminating ribosomes release during the 2-min treatment with translation inhibitors.
source: stop codon peaks are missing from S2 cell samples because terminating ribosomes release during our 2-min treatment with translation inhibitors
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the difference between S2 and embryo samples in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Stop codon peaks are present in embryo samples because embryos are flash-frozen and lysed in the presence of translation inhibitors.
source: They are present in our embryo samples, because these are flash-frozen and lysed in the presence of translation inhibitors, which block termination as well as initiation and elongation
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the presence of termination peaks in embryo data
